Betty Friedan. The American feminist writer whose The Feminine Mystique, published in 1963, ignited second-wave feminism by exposing the unhappiness of educated middle-class women confined to domestic roles.

In that landmark book, she identified what she called the problem that has no name—the dissatisfaction of women who had been told that fulfillment came only through homemaking and motherhood. The book sold over a million copies. Friedan argued that women's identity and true fulfillment required work, education, and independence, not conformity to the feminine ideal that had dominated the 1950s.

In 1966, she co-founded the National Organization for Women, or NOW, and served as its president, mobilizing millions of women around workplace discrimination, reproductive rights, and equal protection under law. Four years later, in 1970, she organized the strike for equality demonstrations, demanding equal pay, accessible childcare, and abortion access. Thousands of women took to the streets. Her work expanded feminism far beyond the suffrage question to encompass sexuality, motherhood, work, and women's sense of identity itself. This was the heart of second-wave feminism.

Later in her career, Friedan faced criticism from more radical feminists who questioned her focus on equality within existing systems rather than transformative social change. Still, she remained one of the most visible and influential faces of women's liberation.
